text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Saturday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Nepalese Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba and Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto held talks on bilateral issues and discussed ways to increase cooperation between the two countries.
- An official of the Pakistani High Commission in New Delhi said he had been tortured by the Indian intelligence agencies.

- Pakistan rejected an Indian protest over the alleged manhandling and expulsion of one of its embassy personnel saying "the concern expressed by the Indian ministry of external affairs is misplaced".

- An International Monetary Fund team has started a review of the Pakistani economy, focusing on taxing agricultural income, cutting defence spending, improving the balance of payments, restricting monetary growth and reducing the budget deficit and cutting inflation to single digits.
- The State (central) Bank of Pakistan plans to impose capital adequacy requirement on all banks from the beginning of 1997.
- Pakistan is expected to negotiate an enhanced structural adjustment facility of about $1.3 billion in February 1997.
- The government has lost about 35 million rupees revenue due to huge smuggling of tea in the first quarter of 1996/97.
- Karachi stocks surged after the IMF team okayed the government's economic and financial stabilisation package.
- A big cabinet reshuffle is expected this month.
- Germany will stop importing Pakistani carpets from January due to non-enforcement of the rug mark system authenticating that the carpet was not made by a child or using forced labour.

- A spokesman of the Pakistan People's Party (Murtaza Bhutto faction) said the party will not allow British detectives to exhume the body of party's slain leader Murtaza Bhutto and threatened legal action if any one tried to desecrate the body.
